questions.disclaimer: Share of a state's public road bridges rated in Poor condition under the FHWA NBI (formerly 'structurally deficient'). Includes Washington DC.
High-Hazard-Potential dams are those whose failure would likely cause loss of human life, regardless of dam size or current condition. Includes Washington DC.
Unlinked passenger trips per resident, all reported transit modes. State totals derived from NTD agency reports. Includes Washington DC.
State average price per gallon of regular unleaded. Prices reflect state-level taxes, transportation costs, and fuel-blend requirements. Includes Washington DC.
Route miles of freight railroad (Class I, regional, and short line), not track miles. Route mileage counts a rail corridor once regardless of parallel tracks. Includes Washington DC.
Landmarks that span more than one state are counted once for each state they touch, so state totals include a small amount of double-counting. Includes Washington DC.
A handful of landmarks span two states and are counted for each state they touch. Includes Washington DC.

Only formally designated National Parks are counted (not National Monuments, Preserves, or Recreation Areas). Multi-state parks are credited to the state where the highest in-park summit lies. DC not included (source omits it).

Excludes lakes that cross state or international borders (Great Lakes, Lake Champlain, Lake Tahoe, Lake Powell, Kentucky Lake, Toledo Bend, Lake Mead, etc.). Great Salt Lake and Salton Sea are included despite being saline. Includes Washington DC.
Percent forested is computed on land area only (excluding inland water). US territories such as American Samoa are excluded from this state-only ranking. Includes Washington DC.
County-equivalent divisions (parishes, boroughs, and independent cities) are counted alongside counties. States that combine a county and an independent city count both. Includes Washington DC.
Range equals the state high point minus the state low point. States with sub-sea-level low points get a small boost in range from the negative minimum. Includes Washington DC.
Only official single-state fairs are counted here; regional/multi-state exhibitions (such as the New England Big E) are excluded. Includes Washington DC.
Measures absolute forest land in acres, not percent of state forested. FIA counts all forested land (public, private, and tribal). Includes Washington DC.

Wilderness areas that cross state boundaries have their acreage split by state. Six states (Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, Kansas, Maryland, Rhode Island) contain no designated wilderness. DC not included (source omits it).

Refuges that span two states are attributed to the state where the main visitor entrance is located. Wetland Management Districts (in some Midwestern states) are included alongside refuges. Includes Washington DC.
Includes all ski areas with lift-served terrain, from major destination resorts down to small local hills. Only 37 US states host any operating ski areas. Includes Washington DC.
A river is credited to every state it flows through, whether as source, mouth, or intermediate section. Only main-stem rivers 500 miles or longer are counted. DC not included (source omits it).
Counts only formally designated National Parks (not monuments, preserves, or historic sites). Multi-state parks have their acreage split at the state boundary. DC not included (source omits it).
Counts standalone aquariums plus aquarium sections of zoos and science centers as listed in the source. Includes both open and recently closed facilities. Includes Washington DC.
